title: Who runs East West Rail and how will it be delivered?
label: 4 November 2026 · Accountability, delivery and governance
summary: The committee questioned East West Rail (EWR) leaders, Network Rail and DfT sponsors about the 744‑day suspension of passenger services on phase 1, lessons for future phases, the programme timetable and costs, freight capacity, electrification choices, consultation and immediate steps to open the line. Witnesses said the infrastructure is built, the dispute has reputational and community costs, EWR is working to be the system ‘conductor’, an outline business case and DCO work are due next year, and Ministers must decide funding and traction solutions.

glossary.definition: Development Consent Order — the planning permission process for major infrastructure projects.
Outline Business Case — the document that sets out the project scope, estimated costs and benefits before major commitment.
Great British Rail — the planned single body to run and plan the national rail network.
Benefit-Cost Ratio — a standard transport appraisal number that compares monetised benefits to costs.
Gross Value Added — a measure of local economic output.
A modern form of construction contract used to share risk and incentivise delivery.
Installing wire in parts of a route while trains use batteries or other power in unwired gaps.
An electric multiple-unit train with batteries to bridge sections without overhead wire.
New law changing pre-application consultation and examination for nationally significant infrastructure projects.

chapters.title: Immediate impact of the dispute on phase 1
chapters.takeaway: Passenger services on phase 1 have been suspended for 744 days; infrastructure is in place but the dispute has reputational and local economic costs.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The line opened but no passenger services have run for 744 days. What has that dispute done to timetable, costs and planning for later phases?

turns.speaker: David Hughes
turns.text: Materially, the delay to passenger operations on phase 1 hasn't changed the planning or costs for future phases. But it has damaged the programme's reputation and hurt local people who expected to use the line.

turns.speaker: Jodie Lofthouse
turns.text: We delivered the phase 1 infrastructure on time and under the £1.2bn funding envelope. Ministers are aware of the lost revenue and we can provide more detail in writing about financial impacts.

turns.speaker: Christian Irwin
turns.text: Network Rail delivered the infrastructure and continues to maintain it. Freight and charter trains run, driver training is active, and we believe the physical railway is ready for passengers when commercial issues are resolved.

turns.speaker: Dr Arthur
turns.text: The public and taxpayers want a team effort to resolve the dispute. How does the lost revenue compare with whatever costs a union settlement might require?

turns.speaker: Jodie Lofthouse
turns.text: I don't have those precise settlement or lost-revenue figures in front of me; we'll follow up in writing. Operational changes also affect the whole system and Ministers must weigh those consequences.

chapters.title: Changing how the project is structured and lessons learned
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses say the key lesson is clearer accountability and treating East West Rail as a whole system, not just infrastructure.

turns.speaker: David Hughes
turns.text: A central lesson is clarity of accountability. For future phases East West Rail Ltd will be responsible for the whole system—'conductor of the orchestra'—not just the tracks.

turns.speaker: Ben Rule
turns.text: You must involve people who operate railways right from the start: rolling stock, depots, training and regulator authorisations have to be planned early, not left to the end.

turns.speaker: Christian Irwin
turns.text: Network Rail's delivery approach learned to focus on outcomes as well as infrastructure. The project saved money during construction and we want to apply the lessons across other large rail programmes.

turns.speaker: Rosemary Hopkins
turns.text: DfT has refreshed sponsorship, with a named SRO, cross‑Whitehall governance and peer support to avoid repeating mistakes seen on HS2 and other projects.

turns.speaker: Dr Arthur
turns.text: Would things have been different if Network Rail ran the whole project from the start?

turns.speaker: Christian Irwin
turns.text: Some issues were about the programme focus. Industrywide, we've moved from infrastructure-only thinking to managing the full passenger outcome; that's the lesson, whoever leads delivery.

chapters.title: Timetable, consents and the business case
chapters.takeaway: EWR expects to present its OBC in mid‑2027 and submit the DCO around the same period. Completion for the full route is expected in the mid‑to‑late 2030s, though estimates are being finalised.

turns.speaker: Olly Glover
turns.text: Earlier plans suggested much faster delivery. How confident are you about current dates for Bedford–Cambridge and the DCO timetable?

turns.speaker: David Hughes
turns.text: Our best estimate now is main works won't start until 2029–30 at the earliest. We'll present the Outline Business Case (OBC) and our draft DCO material to Government around June/July next year.

turns.speaker: Olly Glover
turns.text: And the Full Business Case (FBC)?

turns.speaker: David Hughes
turns.text: FBC would come after DCO award, with major works following—our current schedule points to completion in the mid‑late 2030s but we are still maturing cost and programme assumptions.

turns.speaker: Daniel Francis
turns.text: The NAO said in 2023 the project offered poor value for money. Do you still hold that view?

turns.speaker: Rosemary Hopkins
turns.text: We are preparing the OBC that will quantify transport benefits. But EWR is primarily the backbone of an economic growth strategy for the Oxford–Cambridge corridor; GVA to 2050 is estimated in the business case work.

turns.speaker: David Hughes
turns.text: I have confidence in the strategic business case: housing, jobs and agglomeration effects. The standard BCR metric used in transport appraisal understates growth projects' wider benefits.

chapters.title: Freight capacity and the electrification debate
chapters.takeaway: EWR says the line has capacity for an hourly freight train but other network constraints limit flows; DfT and EWR favour discontinuous electrification with battery trains to decarbonise at lower capital cost, but MPs probed costs and suitability for high‑speed services.

turns.speaker: Dr Arthur
turns.text: Your consultation says up to one freight train per hour—does that mean an hourly guaranteed train?

turns.speaker: Ben Rule
turns.text: We have designed capacity for an hourly freight train, but whether freight operators use it depends on demand and investments elsewhere on the network to unlock routes they need.

turns.speaker: Olly Glover
turns.text: You're proposing discontinuous electrification with battery EMUs. Critics say full electrification is better for freight and long‑term resilience—why choose discontinuous?

turns.speaker: Ben Rule
turns.text: Discontinuous electrification reduces upfront capital cost and avoids complex, expensive works like raising or burying national grid lines at many crossings. DfT's rolling stock strategy supports battery EMUs as the lower‑cost route to a decarbonised passenger service.

turns.speaker: David Hughes
turns.text: When I arrived the assumption was diesel traction. That isn't acceptable for a new 2030s railway. Discontinuous electrification lets us achieve decarbonised passenger traction at a cost Government is prepared to fund.

turns.speaker: Olly Glover
turns.text: But other countries electrify more of their network. Have your costs per track km and your battery rolling stock lease assumptions been peer reviewed?

turns.speaker: Ben Rule
turns.text: We have had external expert panels advise on electrification and we model lease costs for battery EMUs in a range, including higher lease costs than standard EMUs. We'll write with detailed cost assumptions.

turns.speaker: Christian Irwin
turns.text: Electrification costs have fallen in places but stay high in congested urban areas with complex structures and utilities. Battery solutions have real merits where full wiring is disproportionate; the industry is testing and benchmarking options.

chapters.title: Consultation, local engagement and operational details
chapters.takeaway: EWR says it undertook multiple consultations and will move to more iterative, targeted engagement under the new Planning and Infrastructure Act; operational items like driver depots and staffing must be planned early.

turns.speaker: Alex Mayer
turns.text: You ran consultations in 2019–26. Will the public see the DCO application next, and will there be targeted engagements?

turns.speaker: David Hughes
turns.text: In a route‑wide sense, yes—the DCO examination is the next formal public stage. The Planning and Infrastructure Act lets us do more targeted, iterative engagement with communities on the issues that matter to them.

turns.speaker: Daniel Francis
turns.text: Some local campaigners said the 2026 consultation lacked openness and detail. How do you respond?

turns.speaker: David Hughes
turns.text: We made clear the 2026 consultation refined design on the chosen route; it was not about re‑choosing the route. We have high response rates and have made design changes based on feedback. We will keep engaging locally.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: There were also concerns about the driver depot and staffing—was Bletchley always the plan?

turns.speaker: Jodie Lofthouse
turns.text: Bletchley was always within scope as the depot location. When operator plans evolved, some early staff trained at other depots until Bletchley was ready. The point remains: depot and staffing plans must be considered early.

turns.speaker: Ben Rule
turns.text: Exactly. Operational functions must be lined up with infrastructure delivery; bringing operators' operational expertise in early is essential to avoid late blockers.

chapters.title: Next steps and actions to open phase 1
chapters.takeaway: EWR will present its OBC and DCO material next summer and continue design work; resolving the commercial dispute to enable passenger services on phase 1 depends on Chiltern, unions and Ministers, while Network Rail continues final station and staffing tasks.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What immediate steps will you take to get passenger services running on phase 1 as soon as possible?

turns.speaker: David Hughes
turns.text: EWR is not leading the commercial negotiations over operational start—Chiltern is. We will support where needed but the line's physical readiness is not the blocker.

turns.speaker: Jodie Lofthouse
turns.text: DfT is supporting Chiltern and the unions. The Department wants services running and will continue to push for a agreement that gives confidence on entry into service dates.

turns.speaker: Christian Irwin
turns.text: Network Rail is finalising practical tasks: station leases (Winslow), staff contracts for station platforms, and submitting evidence to our internal systems review so the stations can open safely once a go‑live date is set.

turns.speaker: Joe Morris
turns.text: Is retaining East West Rail Co as a separate body still under consideration?

turns.speaker: David Hughes
turns.text: A governance review considered folding EWR into Network Rail or GBR. Ministers and the review decided to keep EWR Ltd as a focused, single‑purpose body for now, but the question may be revisited once the DCO is secured and GBR is standing up.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you. Please send the requested figures and clarifications in writing; the Committee will follow up with the Rail Minister in December.
